title: The famous ‘Face on Mars’ is a two-kilometre mesa that only looked like a face

cover.alt: A grainy 1976 Viking 1 orbiter photograph of the Cydonia region of Mars; a mesa at the top left resembles a human face.

body: On 25 July 1976 the Viking 1 orbiter photographed a mesa in the Cydonia region of Mars. In the grainy, low-resolution frame, lit from the side, the hill looked uncannily like a human face, and the picture became a favourite of people convinced that Mars once had a civilisation. NASA’s chief Viking scientist, Gerald Soffen, called it a trick of light and shadow. Sharper images from Mars Global Surveyor in 2001 and the HiRISE camera in 2007 showed an ordinary eroded hill. Seeing faces in random patterns is called pareidolia, and human brains do it constantly.

slides.alt: A sharp orbital photograph of an eroded mesa on Mars, with the blurry 1976 Viking image of the same hill inset in one corner.
slides.caption: The same hill seen by the HiRISE camera in 2007, with the 1976 Viking image inset. The jump in resolution dissolves the face.
slides.credit: NASA / JPL / University of Arizona · Public domain

slides.question: How many metres of ground did one pixel of the 1976 Viking image cover?
slides.explanation: About 50 metres per pixel. Mars Express images of the same area reach 14 metres per pixel or better, and the face dissolves.

slides.heading: Metres of Mars in one pixel
slides.note: Mars Express images of Cydonia reach 14 m per pixel or better

slides.heading: Why we see faces everywhere
slides.text: Pareidolia is the tendency to see meaningful patterns, especially faces, in random input. Faces matter so much to us that the brain reads two eyes and a mouth into the barest hints: in clouds, in electrical sockets, on the front of a car, and in a shadowed hill on Mars.

HiRISE on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographs it again

slides.question: How did NASA’s chief Viking scientist explain the face in 1976?
options: A trick of light and shadow
slides.explanation: Gerald Soffen dismissed it as a trick of light and shadow. A second Viking frame, taken 35 orbits later at a different sun angle, still looked face-like enough to keep the story alive.
